speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: REFORESTATION
speechtext:
1.	(a) On the forest reserves in western Canada, comprising over twenty-two million acres, administered by the federal forest service, timber is sold under conditions designed to provide reforestation by natural regeneration. This method is much more economical * and, in the long run, more satisfactory than clear cutting and artificial planting. Areas which have been entirely denuded by exploitation and fire can only be re-established to forest cover by seeding or planting, but, owing to the high cost of this work and the' limitations of the forestry appropriation, only experimental plantations have been made so far.
The total area so planted to date is 325 acres.
The policy of the government is to extend these forest reserves so that eventually they shall include all non-agricultural lands capable of supporting tree growth, and to provide for their maintenance in a forested condition by natural regeneration, except where entirely denuded areas demand artificial methods.
(b)	For the establishment of shelter belts on the farms of the prairie provinces, the forest service has for many years operated two tree planting stations, at Indian Head and Sutherland, Saskatchewan. These stations have a capacity of five to six million trees, and cuttings per year. For encouragement in planting, this stock is distributed free,, except for express charges; the consideration, required of the recipient is that he shall prepare and establish the plantation along definitely approved lines, and that subsequently he will give it the necessary cultivation until it is fully established.
Over a period of 25 years, a total of 80,499,455 deciduous and 1,374,418 conifers have been distributed; 75,141 plantations, aggregating .34,053 acres have been established, of which' 70 per cent have been successful, 15 per cent fairly so, and 15 per cent failures due to improper treatment.
(c)	In eastern Canada the forest service has no administrative responsibility on crown lands, the latter being held by the respective provinces. However, for the purpose of advancing forestry methods, the federal forest
Questions

service conducts experimental and research work relating to the regeneration of timber. In some cases this is done independently, in other cases in co-operation with the provinces or the industries.
2.	The appropriation to the forest service in the last fiscal year was $1,185,000.
(a)	$842,000 is spent in the protection administration and improvement of forest reserves. It is possible to segregate the proportion expended in reforestation as an entity, because the management of these lands, including fire protection, all have a bearing on reforestation.
(b)	$75,600 is spent annually in operation of the tree planting division.
(c)	$50,000 is spent in silvicultural research and experimental work in eastern Canada.
(d)	The balance of the appropriation is
absorbed:	(1) Operation of the Forest Products Laboratories at Montreal and Vancouver, (132,400) these institutions carrying on research and tests on wood and wood products; (2) $233,611 is devoted to fire protection on timber lands of the west not as yet dedicated as forest reserves; and (3) numerous other activities of the forest service aimed at the promotion of forestry throughout the Dominion.
3.	The federal government has full control of forestry matters in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the railway belt and Peace River block in British Columbia. In eastern Canada, permanent experiment stations are established as follows:
(a) Petawawa Military Reserve, Ontario, 133,360 acres; (b) Lake Edward Station, Quebec, 3,200 acres; (c) Lake Tremblant Station, Quebec, 1,500 acres; (d) Lake Kenogami Station, Quebec, 200 acres; (e) Bathurst Station, New Brunswick, 500 acres; (f) Cains River Station, New Brunswick, 200 acres; (g) Salmon River Station, New Brunswick, 400 acres; (h) Miscellaneous areas under temporary control only for limited and specific studies.
The foregoing relates to the work of the federal forest service. The provinces of British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia also operate services which exercise somewhat similar functions on the lands over which they have control.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, April 28, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. R. J. Manion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned at six o'clock last evening I was in the act of saying that our Conservative friends tell us we should not encourage the importation of foreign manufactured goods, that we should produce at home everything which possibly can be produced at home, and so to such a degree discourage international trade. In my humble opinion no greater mistake could be made by any Canadian government. If there is one particular in which this government is entitled to the highest praise, it is its wonderful success in the healthy development of international trade, whereby it demonstrates its faith in the fundamental principles of true economics, namely, that in order successfully to build up markets abroad for our constantly growing surplus of Canadian production of every kind we must also be prepared to accept goods in return. It is a well know fact that high tariff duties will prevent international trade, and thus kill the opportunity for return cargoes, which must be encouraged to obtain reasonably low ocean freights. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) told us the other day that other countries of the world were imposing very much higher tariff duties, and in this way shutting us out of their markets. His statements are not borne out by the facts. When

the hon. gentleman spoke the other day he quoted from a report published in 1924, although in saying that I speak subject to correction. Is he not living in the realms of antiquity! May I recall for his benefit the words of Thomas Carlyle when he said:
The race fo.r life has become intense. The runners are treading on each others' heels. Woe be unto him who stops to tie his shoelaces.
So that while my hon. friend has been tying his shoelaces he has taken too long to do it, and the world is going ahead. While the report from which the hon. gentleman quoted, according to my understanding, was published in 1924-*

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
may I read from a
report, which I think is the latest authentic publication extant, the report of the Trade Commission, under the chairmanship of Sir Arthur Balfour, presented to the Baldwin government in June, 1925?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The report from which I
read was published in 1925 also.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While it is a fact that
at the close of the war foreign countries, more particularly the countries of Europe, did impose high tariff duties, they are beginning to realize the mistake they made by so doing:
The political settlement following the war nearly doubled the number of independent customs administrations in central and eastern Europe, and also that the administration of restrictions has been largely in the hands of comparatively new arid inexperienced authorities; the burden thus imposed on trade will be readily imagined.
Nor is it necessary for us to pronounce any opinion on the justification or efficiency of the measures taken during a period of abnormal crisis.
The report goes on to say:
We therefore rejoice to note that there is now a tendency to recognize the evil effects of customs prohibitions as an instrument of fiscal policy, and to reduce the number of such prohibitions towards the minimum necessary to ensure public security, health and morals, and other objects of essential national importance. Since the latter port of 1923 great progress has been made in Czechoslovakia in removing restrictions, and that Hungary removed all her import restrictions at the beginning of 1925. The intention of Germany to sweep away the greater part of her prohibitions is expressed in the recent Anglo-German treaty. In France, Italy, Poland, and a number of other foreign states few obstacles at present remain to British trade arising from import prohibitions.
And then the report makes this statement:
The conclusion emerges that, taken as a whole, the ad valorem incidence of overseas tariffs on British goods has slightly declined since 1914.
Then again:
The board of trade calculation brings out clearly the remarkable fact that the main increases of tariff rates

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
on British exports have been within the British Empire, where the average ad valorem incidence has risen, by nearly two-thirds, while dn foreign countries, despite the great increase in the United States tariff, the average ad valorem incident has decreased by one-fifth, the net result, on balance, being a slight decline, as stated above.
The figures speak for themselves, and may I also say that aided by the handi of a beneficent Providence, and under the wise direction of the King government, fortified as it is by such a noble band of true and loyal supporters, not only to my right but behind the government, Canada's international trade will not refuse to grow. This is shown by the following figures: During the four years since this government assumed the reins of power our entire foreign trade has risen from 81,501.000.000 in 1921-22 to over $2,255,000,000 for the year ending March 31 last, or an increase during those four years under the present government of over $750,000,000. Furthermore we have the very favourable condition that exists to-day, a favourable trade balance of over $401,000,000, and what is still better, our Canadian dollar is away above par on the New York exchange. Consider this present condition of Canadian trade with what it was during the last full year of the Meighen government wdien we had an unfavourable trade balance of over $29,000,000, and the Canadian dollar was worth only eighty-five cents on the New York exchange.
We have heard a great deal from hon. members across the way regarding the unpatriotic and most radical expressions which emanate from our friends of the Progressive party. I have no brief for the Progressive members but I resent any insinuations that the opinions which they have expressed in this Plouse will not tend in the highest degree towards the progress and betterment of this country. These men from the west-both Liberal and Progressives-as well as my hon. friends further to my left, represent the very soul of honour, and they have shown us that they have the highest and truest interests of this country at heart. No wonder when our friends of the Progressive party had a chance to come in and view the situation, and when they saw the band of men over here behind such a leader, they said: "There are the kind of fellows we want to co-operate with."
This question of international trade has become a burning problem in the United States of America. Many writers and economists there are beginning to ask how long * a nation can continue to sell goods abroad without making purchases. The majority opinion is insistent that gold cannot be piled up indefinitely, and that pay must be taken
in goods if the foreign trade of the country is to be maintained. As the situation in the United States stands to-day, it is only a question of time when they must radically change their present policy of high protection. They are faced with the necessity of holding their foreign trade markets and also with the greater difficulty of safeguarding some $9,500,000,000 invested in other countries, the payment of which can only be effectively secured through the medium of returning trade. The American government to-day is now spending over $3,500,000 annually to retain those foreign trade markets, and even at that it finds those markets slipping away. In view of the following facts:
1.	That the American government will be compelled to open her markets to foreign goods, and materially modify her international trade policy in order to safeguard her enormous investments abroad.
2.	That her people need and will continue to need in greater quantity much of our Canadian surplus of agricultural productions.
3.	That freedom to that great consuming population with so many wealthy people would open the world's best market right at our own door.
4.	That it would be a real solution of our economic maritime difficulties.
5.	The fact that in the face of the high tariff walls now existing between these two countries, over $1,070,000,000 worth of trade out of our entire foreign trade of $2,255,000,000 is now done with the American people shows: first, that the people of both countries are desirous of encouraging further mutually beneficial trade, and second, it shows the power of natural trade laws, which is an indication of the only rational trade policy. Therefore, I urge the government to do everything in reason to cultivate the most friendly relations with the American government, with a view to arranging for favourable trade relations between the two countries whenever the opportunity may afford; and to that end, the Canadian government should have its trade representative in Washington. I urge this the more because in 1911 the United States government passed an act giving to Canada reciprocal trade in cattle, and a nominal tax of one-quarter cent per pound of beef. That provision remained in force for eleven years. In 1915 congress put cattle and beef on the free list, giving our Canadian farmers the benefit of that great open market. At the same time they placed wheat, flour, and potatoes on the tentative free list. Canada during those years never showed any apprecia-

The Budget-Mr. McMillan
tion, but kept an ad valorem duty of 25 per cent against American cattle and three cents a pound against American beef. After such treatment the American government quite naturally withdrew the provision. Of course Canada had then a Conservative government in power.
In the case of such an arrangement as I have indicated, care must be taken-and this government deserves credit for having taken every precaution-to preserve the health of Canadian herds. The department must also be ready to grapple with any destructive pests and to prevent them getting a foothold through importations. Consider the destruction the corn borer has wrought because precautions were not taken in time. There is also the bean weavil, and other pests, and it is the urgent duty of the government to go the limit, if need be, even to place an embargo on any foreign importations which might endanger the health and success of this profitable and most desirable crop.
The more we study the problem of Canadian agriculture and the vital necessity of placing and maintaining on the land a sufficient farm population, the more do we realize that the problem is basic and all-important to the progress and development of the nation. Although it may seem almost chimerical, yet what is needed in this country is such a readjustment of national ideas, as will place agriculture and its claims to the best intelligence and the highest skill of our people in the very forefront of national thought; and when this re-awakening is sufficiently emphatic, there will then be no more hastening away from the farm, but rather such a just conception of agriculture as our main resource and our most dignified and independent vocation as will attract to its just aim in the improvement of methods, the increase of yields and the clearing away of the unjust economic obstructions which lie across its path, the wisdom and the science and the willing hands of millions who may then obtain a just remuneration for their labour, and also be able to hand on to posterity an unimpaired inheritance.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I admire the courage of
my hon. friend. He impresses me as being a man of convictions, and having the courage to stand up and declare those convictions

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
much more freely and definitely than most men holding his views. I am always able to get along with a man who has convictions, and who will stand by them. It is the wobbler with whom it is hard to get along. My hon. friend charged this party with insincerity and I will deal with that a little later on.
He quoted Mr. Henry Ford as an advocate of free trade. Mr. Henry Ford has made about two billion dollars under protection; he has put himself into a position of financial strength that enables him now to say: I can make machines under free trade and I believe there ought to be free trade. He would do now what the British people did. In Great Britain they had protection until their industrial supremacy was established, and when that time arrived they said: Now let us have free trade. That is exactly the position of Mr. Ford to-day. I do not think a man who has made two billion dollars under a protective policy is one who can be quoted favourably as an advocate of free trade. I would ask my hon. friend: What did free trade do for the farmers of Britain? Is British agriculture in a state of prosperity today? Has it been in a state of prosperity for forty years?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That cannot be answered in a word. The British farmers have been able to show to the world what we ought to do in regard to live stock production and they are not dependent on their own production of agricultural foodstuffs. For twenty years I went back and forth and I am conversant with conditions in Great Britain. The best farmers there are doing as I have been doing all my life. They have never been selling one cent's worth of agricultural produce, unless it is a little wheat. In addition to what they grow they are buying largely of foodstuffs from foreign lands and feeding animals on their own farms, in this way building up agriculture to the highest possible extent. The British farmers to-day are able to show to the world that they can lead the world, more particularly in live stock production.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think I ought to remind the hon. member that we are not in the corner store in the town of Seaforth and a discussion in parliament is conducted in a somewhat different manner. The fact however remains that about forty per cent of British land capable of being tilled is in grass, and there can be no doubt that the agricultural industry in Britain is, and has been for forty years past, greatly depressed. If free trade is good for the farmers in Canada, why is it not good for the farmers in Great Britain? The farmers
of the United States are more prosperous in that most highly protected country in the world than the farmers of Great Britain. Those who argue in favour of free trade for the farmers ought to cast their minds a little further than the horizon bounded by the county of Huron. Let them look over the world and find out where the farmer is prosperous; let them view the tariff conditions under which those farmers live, and I submit it will be found that the most prosperous farmers are to be found in protectionist countries.
I was sorry to hear my hon. friend belittle the fruit and vegetable grower, who is a land holder of small dimensions but who is one who works harder than any farmer in the west, harder than most farmers in the east. The only way in which a man can make a living on a fruit and vegetable farm is by bending his back and cultivating every inch of his land. These men are maintaining families on ten and twenty acres. You can go througn all the older part of Ontario and you.will find fruit and vegetable growers with ten to twenty acres, maintaining as many people on that acreage as are to be found on 200-acre farms in other parts of the province or in the west. Surely that man, who works not part of the year but every day of the year and who maintains his family on a small acreage, is entitled to just as much, if not a little more, credit than the man who has a large area of land to cultivate.
My hon. friend became quite eloquent in discussing the burdens that are placed upon the poor working people of the towns and cities by a protective policy. How does he account for the fact that about ninety per cent of these poor working people, these poor mechanics and others with their little homes and families, voted for a protective tariff on the 29th October last? Throughout all industrial Canada with the exception of Quebec-and conditions there were somewhat peculiar, because the policy voted upon in that province was not the fiscal policy of the country at all

the issue was the tariff. In the province of Quebec the issue was conscription. In Manitoba, in the Maritimes, in Ontario and in British Columbia the issue was the tariff, and in every industrial centre the people voted strongly for the policy of Imy right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen). If, therefore, the poor people for whom my hon. friend is so highly concerned know what is best for themselves, it is quite clear that they believe in the policy of protection. My hon. friend may talk free trade in this House, as Michael Clark of Red Deer, did, session in and session out, and he will make no impression upon the
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

government nor upon the country. The people who have the intelligence to see the situation in which we are placed, alongside a highly protected nation competing with us in so many things, will agree that the protective policy is necessary for Canada.
The budget has evidently been prepared for the purpose of impressing the public of Canada with the idea that this country is prosperous, and that it was prosperous last year. A substantial reduction is made in taxation, and it is attributed by the government, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), to the increased prosperity that prevailed in the year 1925. I maintain, however, that the country is not prosperous; it was not prosperous last year nor the year before, and it is not prosperous to-day. But to make my point I will take the figures of the railways. There is no better barometer of trade than the railways; if trade is good traffic is good, and if traffic is good the railways are prosperous. I find, as I have discovered myself, that business depression has reflected in the railway reports was more severe in 1925 than in 1924, and I take the ground that the relief in taxation afforded by this budget is by no means equal to the extra burdens put upon the people of the country by the government.
I take the report of the Canadian Pacific Railway and from it I quote the following:
The gross earnings for the year increased $853,849 over those of the previous year. Working expenses, however, decreased $2,073,684, resulting in net earnings, before deducting fixed charges, of $40,154,775.
The report goes on to say:
The relatively small increase an gross earnings is largely accounted for by the depression which existed in Canada during the first part of the year, the effects of which in general traffic were only overcome by the excellent harvest, to which is largely due an increase of $10,354,946 in the gross earnings during the last half of the year over the corresponding period of 1924.
But for the abundant harvest, therefore, the earnings of Canadian Pacific Railway would have been $10,000,000 less than the year-previous. If that is an evidence
4 p.m. of prosperity I should like to have it explained to me by some member who has a keener mind than I possess. It is to my mind absolute proof that the year 1925 was not equal to that of 1924. The same report goes on to say:
From a shipping standpoint the year 1925 .... was perhaps the worst of which there is record, and the result of the operations of your Atlantic and Pacific fleets were unsatisfactory, particularly in passenger revenue. The number of immigrants carried by all lines was less by over 40,000 than in 1924. Notwithstanding a decrease in expenses of $706,951 the net earnings from all traffic were substantially less than those of the previous year.

So that the opinion of this great railway company, upon whose board there are some of the ablest businessmen in Canaan, is that the year 1925 was much less prosperous than the year 1924. I notice from the report that the grain traffic carried by the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1925 was 263,000.000 bushels or 31,000,000 bushels more than in 1924.
I will admit that agriculture was more prosperous in Canada in 1925 than in 1924. but the fact is that general business suffered more serious depression. And that fact is borne out by the railway figures.
I take the Canadian National Railway report in which some interesting disclosures are made. For example, I find the following statement:
The results for 1925 may be regarded as generally satisfactory and were due to a combination of increased gross earnings and decreased expenses. From January to June inclusive, the gross earnings in 1925 were less than for the corresponding months in 1924. The movement of the large western crop made itself felt towards the end of the year with a consequent increase in gross revenue of 3.9 per cent for the year. In the face of the decreased business which obtained during the greater part of 1925, every effort in the direction of economy was put forth and maintained throughout the whole of the year. These efforts resulted in a decrease in expenses for the year of $5,637,143.25.
So that it was due to the efficient management of the Canadian National Railways that the showing was so favourable this year. I find in the same report that the Dominion government's estimate for all grains in the Canadian grain crop for the calendar year 1925 was 1,126,113,000 bushels or an increase of 33.5 per cent in the crop. In other words, the farmers of Canada in 1925 had 375.371,034 bushels more than in 1924. That includes all grains, and it is fair to assume that on the average the grain crop would run about $1 per bushel. We may therefore fairly estimate that $300,000,000 was earned by the farmers of Canada last year in excess of the year before. Yet the railways in their general traffic did not do nearly so well as they did in the previous year. The report of the Canadian National Railways makes this statement: The grain movement to the head of the lakes was increased by 9.9 per cent, and in addition to that 9,000,000 bushels were shipped out at Vancouver. It will be found that this movement of grain accounts for all the increase that was enjoyed by the two great railway systems of the country. My argument, therefore, is that the traffic arising from sources other than the carriage of farm products was substantially less in 1925 than in the year before, so that in consequence we had a greater degree of general business de-

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
pression last year. Take the passenger earnings of the railways. The passenger earnings of the Canadian National Railways decreased by $615,516. The number of passengers carried by the Canadian National Railway system last year showed a decrease of 1,032.641, or 4.5 per cent.
We all rejoice in the growing prosperity of our national railway system, but the credit for this belongs-I do not think the government will be bold enough to claim it- to the efficiency of the management and to the loyalty of the 95,000 employees. This efficiency is indicated by the fact that with an increase of $9,000,000 in gross earnings

all from the abundant harvest-there was a decrease of $6,000,000 in operating cost.
I should like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the depression in general traffic resulted in a decrease last year of slightly over 3,000 employees on the Canadian National Railways and of 1,500 on the Canadian Pacific Railway. So that railway employees to the number of 4,500 lost their positions, or, if not, they worked half or part time. When 4,500 men connected with these two great railway enterprises, employing in the case of the Canadian National
98,000	men and, I presume, a proportionate number for the smaller mileage of the Canadian Pacific, are without work for a year, or are working only half time, it cannot be argued that this country is in a prosperous condition.
But, Sir, I think of all Canadians my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) should rejoice most over the prosperity of the Canadian National Railways. As was pointed out by my	hon.	friend	from	SouthWellington (Mr. Guthrie), the right hon. gentleman had	a	desperate	fight	beforehe succeeded	in	merging	the	Grand
Trunk and the Canadian Northern into one great national railway system. He was not assisted by hon. gentlemen opposite. I sat in the House during that period and I know the pessimism that prevailed among the Liberal party with regard to the future of the Canadian National Railways, and that pessimism has continued almost down to the present day. But in spite of all the opposition which he encountered the right hon. leader of this party perservered in his efforts and succeeded in establishing this great railway enterprise-a railway system run by the people and for the people. To-day, Sir, we see it rapidly approaching the time when, as he predicted, it will meet all its fixed charges, and become a valuable asset. Indeed, a prominent railway man has stated that it will be an asset equivalent in value to paying off our national debt.
Mr. Speaker, let me discuss for a moment or two the decrease in taxation. We are told that during the past fiscal year there was an increase in revenue of $29,965,000, in consequence of which the Minister of Finance is relieving the country of $25,000,000 taxation- entirely by reducing the income tax. But I should like to point out to the House that the collections of excise taxes last year amounted to $85,000,000. There are no reductions in those taxes. On the contrary, the sales tax was raised from 3 per cent to 6 per cent by the present government, and afterwards reduced to 5 per cent-at which figure it still stands -as against 3 per cent under the government supported by the Conservative party. That means the government since 1921 has added 40 per cent to our excise taxes. That percentage of $85,000,000 represents $34,000,000. So while the administration say, "We are reducing your taxes by $25,000,000," they stand convicted of having raised the taxes of the people to the extent of $34,000,000, or if we take their estimated figures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1927, $95,000,000, they will collect an additional $38,000,000 of taxation during this period. And yet they ask for the applause of the people. Well, they are not much entitled to it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I doubt that very much.
A government which increases taxation by $39,000,000, and then comes seeking credit for a reduction of $25,000,000, is surely not in a strong position to ask for the thanks of the heavily burdened taxpayers of this country. What the government should have done in addition to decreasing the income tax-and that is something for which the country has been clamouring for a long time as being long overdue-was to cut off that 40 per cent of excise taxes. Then we would have had our taxes approximating very close to those which were collected by the Conservative government. The present administration put on the receipt tax and took it off, and then said, "What a good boy am I!" And that tax was entirely a tax imposed by this government. The cheque tax was added to enormously. Originally under the preceding government it was two cents on all cheques; under this government it is two cents on every fifty dollars. Therefore I submit that the excise tax collected last year was 40 per cent in excess of the sales tax collected in 1921.
I go further, Mr. Speaker, I say that of all taxes collected the most burdensome is the sales tax. It is felt most heavily by the consumer, it is felt in every home, and when it is
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

finally paid it comes close to a 10 per cent tax on many of the necessaries of life. It i3 a more grievous tax to bear than the income tax-which does not touch the average home- or the tariff tax, which if it falls at all on the people at least gives them in return steady employment; and without steady employment, even if one had no taxes to pay he would still be poor indeed. So that the tax felt most seriously by the people is the sales tax, which this government has increased to an extent equivalent to an increased collection of $38,000,000. So I do not give them very much credit for that.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the government is evidently expecting a great deal of gratitude from the people for reducing the taxes on automobiles. My friends to the left have been charged with forcing the government to make that reduction. For myself, I do not think that is the case. The Progressive party made its arrangement with the government at the beginning of the session, and the programme brought down in the Speech from the Throne is the programme which the Progressives insisted upon as being necessary to gain their support. But in connection with this induction in motor duties something happened. There was some other influence brought to bear upon the government, or else the government was simply dealing with those constituencies in which motor factories existed in a fashion that was called by one of that party at one time "cold justice," or, in other words, getting even with them. I think my hon. friends to my left see the wisdom, and the fairness, of the amendment introduced by my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion). His amendment says that before this reduction is made it should be submitted to the Tariff Advisory Board. That is a board of so-called experts, and if they are not experts, they can get expert help.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I would hardly expect this government to submit it to any body but one of its own creation. They would not submit it to the tariff board of 1920 surely; they would not have confidence in them. Apparently they have no confidence in their own board either. They have appointed three men of some eminence in the country, but they have not sufficient confidence in them to submit to them this very first tariff change that comes up for settlement. In the Speech from the Throne there is a direct statement that there would be no reduction in duties, nor interference with the tariff,

until the board of experts had considered each proposed change and made their recommendations. But only a few days afterwards, comparatively speaking, the government go back on their promises and make a cut in the automobile duties the effect of which neither they, their experts, nor any other person can know without a most exhaustive and expert investigation-a cut that, in my opinion, is calculated seriously to impair one of the basic industries of this country. I submit to my friends of the Progressive party that a fair position for them to take is that this question of the duties on motor cars should be submitted to that tariff board. That is all that is being asked in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Fort William. That is not only fair, Mr. Speaker, but that is the record on which my hon. friends of the Progressive party rest to-day.

speechtext:
I would say that on this question my hon. friend ought to be one of the best posted men in the House, because he has given great consideration to tariff reduction, and he ought to be in touch, if not directly, at all events through his leader, with the tariff intentions of the party to which he is for the moment giving his support.

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
We stand to-day, Mr. Speaker, in the position where a great industry in this country, an industry with ramifications through all our commerce, is threatened with serious impairment, and it is threatened without investigation, without taking expert advice, and absolutely contrary to the pledges of the government as contained in the Speech from the Throne.
Just here, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reply to the remark of my hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan), who charged this party with insincerity. Whatever faults we may have on this side, and I am free to confess that we are not quite perfect, we can claim this, at least, that our leader and his followers are sincere in the policies which they present to this House, and they have been all through their existence. What is the record of my hon. friends opposite? I am going to sketch it, Mr. Speaker, for the information of my hon. friend for South Huron. They adopted a platform in 1919 in which the party pledged itself to lower duties. They went to the country in 1921, and they sent their agents among the manufacturers, and told their candidates that they could assure the manufacturers that the duties would not be lowered. First they pledged themselves to the country to reduce duties, and then they go to the men affected and say: We will not reduce the duty. Then they come into this House and sit during two sessions and keep their pledges, not to the country-they break their pledges to the country-but they keep their pledges to the manufacturers. There follows another session, and then comes reduction of duty. They pledge themselves to the country to reduce duties, and they pledge themselves to the manufacturers not to reduce duties. Then they come into the House and they do reduce duties. If my hon. friends can find anything like sincerity in such conduct as that, I am at a loss to understand their mentality. We had the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, Mr. Marler, in the last parliament stand up in this House and declare that he had been authorized by the leaders of the party to tell the manufacturers in his riding that the duties would not be lowered, and he protested most vehemently in this House against the reduction of duties made in the first budget of my hon. friend the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). If that is not insincerity, what is? If that is not a wobbling course, what is a wobbling course? Then we come to this session, and in the Speech from the Throne the government says to the people of this country, to the manufacturers as well as to all others:
Before any reduction in duties is made, the question of each industry shall be submitted to an expert Tariff Advisory Board. But scarcely is the ink dry on the document containing that pledge, before the government brings down a reduction of duties without submitting it to the tariff board. No such insincerity as this, Mr. Speaker, has ever marked the course of any government, or ot any party, since confederation. The government stands convicted by the record, by the statements of their own members, and by their legislation, as a government in which sincerity has no place whatever.
I want particularly to say a few words in behalf of an industry that is making a losing fight for existence in this country. Three years ago I brought before the House this question of protection for the magazine and periodical publishers in Canada, not merely for their sake, Mr. Speaker, but for the sake of Canada, for the sake of the young men and the young women of Canada, to prevent the denationalizing of the spirit of Canada. The late Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding, stood in his place in this House and gave his approval to the suggestions that I then made, but nothing was done. I have brought this question before the House since, but without having any relief given to this industry. A large deputation of men representing this industry came down to Ottawa this session, but they could not get a hearing, so that the government stand to-day with regard to this industry as treating it as one that is of no consequence in Canada.

speechtext:
The statement made is:
We tried to make arrangements with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to bring a delegation down composed of representatives of such national bodies as the Canadian Authors Association, the Canadian Clubs, the I.O.D.E., National Council of Women, Pulp and Paper Association, Ink Makers Association, Engravers Association, Typographical Unions, Canadian Manufacturers Association, Associated Boards of Trade, Association of Canadian advertisers, etc.
The above mentioned ministers could not give us an appointment until after the budget was down.
I propose to show the volume of American periodicals coming into this country and it is simply staggering. That volume has increased from $881,621 in 1912 to $2,776,885 in 1924 and 1925, an increase of 200 per cent in a period of thirteen years. There are over 300 of these publications coming into this country free, and there are over 20,000,000 copies of American made magazines and periodicals entering Canada every year. There are over 20,000,000 copies of twenty-five different publications coming into Canada yearly, while the total circulation of American magazines in this country is over 40,000,000. Foi every' single Canadian magazine purchased in Canada there are eight copies of American magazines purchased. In addition to that, from fifteen to twenty million copies of weekend papers, and of daily papers, published in the United States are coming into this country with all the influence of Americanism which they can exercise. I will give you the Canadian circulation of one paper, a very salacious one. The Buffalo Times circulates 1,460.264 copies in this country every year. I have before me a piece of advertising from that publication which is of the most suggestive and dangerous character. It advertises that it is telling the story of the Princess Chimay and the Hungarian gypsy musician Rigo, with respect to' whom an international scandal prevailed for years. This scandal, in all its nauseating details, is told by the gypsy musician himself. Is that the kind of stuff we ought to have in Canada? We are told that obscene literature can be rejected by the customs. Still, that paper is not barred, and there can hardly be anything worse than the gypsy Rigo story in the Sunday Times.
This tremendous importation of American magazines makes it impossible for Canadian magazines to live. One after another they

are going out of existence and leaving the entire field to American publications. My information, and it comes from an authentic source, is that the Curtis Publishing Company of Philadelphia has opened six branches in Canada lately for promoting the sale of their Saturday Evening Post and their Ladies' Home Journal, and their objective is 500,000 copies of the former magazine every week. That is the objective of the Curtis Publishing Company, and that magazine comes into the country free. It comes in by reason of a conflict of two items in the customs tariff. But it is within the power of this government to cancel one of these items-item 184-and that would leave them in a position to collect 25 per cent duty on that magazine. I have a list here, a copy of which I presume is in the possession of other hon. members, of twenty-five different publications. One of these circulates 145,000 copies a month in Canada, another 113,000, the Saturday Post 101,000 weekly, the Cosmopolitan 69,000, the True Story-one of the most salacious of all the American magazines-90,000, the total being
1,002,000	copies. That is the kind of material coming into Canada without paying duty.
The Saturday Evening Post is a publication of 226 pages of which 40 per cent is reading and 60 per cent advertising matter. If that 60 per cent of this particular publication were sent in without the reading matter it would pay a tax, under our tariff, of fifteen cents a pound, but because it is mixed up with a certain amount of literary matter it is allowed to come in free. It is within the power of the Minister of Customs, with the consent of the government, to remedy this thing to-day, or to-morrow, by making an amendment to the customs tariff eliminating item 184.

speechtext: Would it carry the same weight then as the advertising matter?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, it would carry more. Let me read item 169, of the customs tariff to the following effect:
Books, namely: novels or works of fiction, or literature of a similar character, unbound or paper-bound or in sheets, but not to include Christmas annuals. . . . British preferential tariff, fifteen cents a pound; intermediate tariff 22\ cents a pound; general tariff 25 cents a pound.
That is the item under which this stuff should be imported, but it is not. It is classified under item 184 of the tariff which reads this way:
Newspapers, and quarterly, monthly and semimonthly magazines, and weekly literary papers, unbound	free

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
All that is necessary for this government to do is to wipe out item 184, which in any case absolutely contradicts item 169. The last named item says there shall be a duty on these things; item 184 says there shall not be any duty. But in order to make item 1S4 apply the Minister of Customs has to say that that book is not bound. Now that book is bound, but the Department of Customs says it is not bound. If they said it was bound they would have to pay a tariff of 25 per cent. It is bound as much as a great majority of magazines published in this or in any other country are bound. In my judgment it is a bound book, and should come in as a bound book, but the tariff under which it comes in says that if it is unbound it will come in free, and an arbitrary ruling of the department which has been in existence for many years makes it possible for the American publisher to flood this country with his work, to the detriment, not merely of the public, but of the men who turn out these magazines, of the workmen engaged in the work, and, more than anything else, of the people of Canada who are being Americanized by their reading matter more than by any other or all other influences put together.
But I was going to explain why Canadian publishers cannot compete. In the first place here is a magazine of 262 pages. Every cent of overhead cost in the production of that magazine is paid for by the American circulation. There is a cover that will cost them 81,000 to begin with. Then there are all the editorial expenses, the payment of the writers, all the cost of ilustration, of making plates and all that goes into the preparation of the magazine. This copy coming into Canada does not bear one fraction of a cent of all that cost. It is all borne by the two million circulation in the United States. This is the by-product of a great magazine factory. All the cost they are put to is the paper and the printing that is put in the magazine. The advertiser who pays $7,000 a page for his announcement makes up the difference between the actual cost of the paper and the price for which it is sold in Canada. How can a Canadian magazine compete with that? The publisher here has to pay the cost of editing, the cost of the writers of the articles, and what chance have the Canadian authors to get into Canadian magazines? ' None at all. They have to pay rent and taxes, pay for type setting and everything, and they have to do it in competition with men who do not have to pay any of these expenses. Surely it requires but a moment for a man of perspicacity to realize that while these conditions exist the
Canadian magazine is an impossibility, and I submit the Canadian periodical press is very desirable. But these are not all the handicaps they labour under. The materials that enter into Canadian magazines are all taxed. If they import their paper it is subject to a duty of 25 per cent. If they import ink they have to pay 20 per cent. There is a duty of 20 per cent on engraving and a duty of 20\ per cent on art work. There is a duty from 10 per cent to 25 per cent on machinery and a duty of 15 cents a pound on advertising plates. All these things have to be paid for by Canadian publishers, while they are all covered by their competitors who circulate in competition with them in Canada.
Another feature of it, Mr. Speaker, which to my mind is very interesting is the effect it has upon Canadian goods. In this magazine I have in my hand we have ninety-four pages of advertising-some of the most alluring and attractive advertising that you will find any place in the world, all advertising American products and making a market in Canada for American gooods, and not a single Canadian manufacturer can place his advertisement in that magazine. He will have to pay the cost of two and a half million circulation to get
100,000	circulation. The thing is absolutely prohibitive to the Canadian manufacturer, and it works out, according to one manufacturer whose statement I have here, very injuriously indeed. I will quote from Mr. Newman, chairman of the Picton Board of Trade. He says:
I might mention the county of Prince Edward is putting out about one-half of the canned vegetables manufactured in the Dominion of Canada. The county of Prince Edward puts out the best tomato in the world. Yet we are using ten or twenty times the amount of American-made Campbell's tomato soup, which our country is so famous for producing. The Canadian canners put up a tomato soup the equal of any other, but the American soup is purchased because of the large full page colour advertisements in the American magazines. The housewife looks at that, and it makes her almost hungry for tomato soup, and she goes down town without considering where it is made, or considering that she is employing American labour, and makes her purchase. Or she calls up on the 'phone, and orders Campbell's soup.
I have no interest in any publication; the Prince Edward Board of Trade is not interested in a publication, but we are interested in that demand which American publications are creating in Canada for American-made goods, and the fact that Canadians are using so much of the class of goods which can be just as well purchased in Canada.
That is the effect, according to the chairman of the Picton Board of Trade, upon one industry. I do not think there is an hon. member in this House, who, from his own experience, does not know that what Mr. Newman says is absolutely correct, and if it affects all our industries similarly, is it any
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

wonder that there is business depression in Canada? Our manufacturers cannot get their product advertised, while their American competitors have the most attractive advertising to be found in any country in the world, these advertisements are put into the homes of Canadians duty free and their goods are thus put into competition with Canadian goods. I have a statement here which says that over 25,000,000 pounds of advertising comes into Canada each year in these publications. If that came in unmixed with a little literary matter it would be subject to a duty of 15 cents a pound, but they mix it up, and they get an arbitrary interpretation of a certain clause in the customs tariff, and in it comes, to drive out of employment the workmen who would otherwise be engaged in such work, and to ruin scores of publishers, to my certain knowledge, who have endeavoured to establish Canadian magazines. In that way this whole country is left to the mercy of Americans promulgating their own ideas of nationality, and their own ideas, sometimes, of morality. I will quote another author, Colonel Owen Lobley, of the Holland Varnish Company, a large Canadian manufacturer who, speaking on the menace of imported advertising, said:
Gentlemen, the popular foreign magazine is one of the most powerful and pernicious aids to peaceful penetration. Persistent advertisements attract the attention of our families to foreign products. Stories and articles are moulding the minds of our young people along American lines, and towards American ideas and ideals. What progress can a "Produced-in-Canadacompaign make against resistance such as this?
And I will give you a quotation from an American source, none other than J. I. Britain, United States Consul General at Winnipeg. Speaking of the American magazine advertising he says:
The advertisements in -these magazines are perused with considerable advantage to the advertiser as they keep before the public numerous lines of American merchandise.
These are authorities, these are men who have been up against it and who are entitled to speak. During the past few years these Canadian publications, in addition to others, have been driven out of existence: Canadian Weekly, Canadian Courier, Women's Century, Pictorial Review, Every-woman's World, The Listening Post, and a host of relatively smaller publications. The effect of this is understood by national and social societies of the country. The National Council of Women passed this resolution:
Whereas, the efforts of the Canadian Magazine Association to have a duty placed upon United States magazines are entirely in line with the resolutions of the I.O.D.E. adopted at the annual meeting; be it therefore resolved that we, the national executive

heartily endorse the action of the Canadian Magazine Association and pray the government to take early and favourable action thereon.
This is one by the Canadian Club:
Resolved:	That our executive is of the opinion that
every effort should be made to encourage literary effort in Canada, and it is felt that a protective tariff on imported magazines, more particularly those from the United States, would result in lessening the importation of magazines many of which are of an undesirable type and would promote the production of Canadian magazines edited from the Canadian viewpoint.
I might go on with quotations from the Typographical Union, manufacturers' associations and others who are more or less affected by the flooding of Canada with this pernicious kind of literature. There is no desire, no intention to exclude, and a tax would not have the effect of excluding any good United States magazines. A duty of ten or fifteen cents a pound on the Century or Harpers' Monthly or any other good magazine would not be a serious tax and would not prevent them from coming into this country. People in Canada who want that type of magazine would be glad to pay for it, if in return they could secure the exclusion of the villainous literature that comes in duty free at the present time.
One thing I object to is the utter disregard of the present government for the welfare of this country as it is affected by this importation of United States magazines. I myself have been arguing the matter for four years. My arguments met with the sympathetic approval of the Minister of Finance, and I have yet to be told by any member of the government or any member of the party that the restriction of this flood of United States literature would be unwise. They all agree with me but they will not do anything. Surely this is something that should have the sympathetic attention of a government that wants to keep Canada a part of the British Empire, that wants to keep Canada from annexation to the United States. How long can we stand the literary penetration of this country by United States writers? That is a question that my hon. friends should ask themselves. How far is this responsible for the exodus from this country to the United States, which is painted to our young men and young women as a land of promise, with higher wages, better conditions and good times?

speechtext:

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know intimately the
publisher of MacLean's Magazine and I know the proprietor; there is no stronger advocate of the duty on United States magazines than he is.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That may
be, but he reprints stories out of Hearst's Cosmopolitan.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member will nnd that they are written by Canadian writers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and he is using the
clause in the Copyright Act by which he can get possession of these stories. He is paying royalties to Canadian writers who sell their product first to United States magazines, and why? Mr. Stringer and other Canadian writers can sell their stories to the Cosmopolitan and other United States magazines for five times the price that any Canadian publisher can afford to pay. Naturally they go there, and until the Copyright Act was changed and it was made possible for a Canadian publisher to get a license to publish anything that was published in United States and was refused publication in Canada, Mr. Stringer's work could not be published in Canada; it appeared only in the paper that bought it. But under present conditions of the Copyright Act, MacLean's Magazine or any other magazine can go to headquarters and say: I want a license to publish that, and the authorities of the Copyright branch will say: We will give you a license and you pay tMe author so much. It is possible now to force United States magazines to have these Canadian writers' articles published in Canada. What is the result? Canadian publishers do not have to take out a license. The fact that it is possible for them to get a license enables them to make an arrangement with United States publishers to get stories of Canadian writers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In this matter I have a
good deal of sympathy with the position the hon. gentleman has taken; but from the standpoint of peaceful penetration of Canada with United States ideals is it not the case that the magazines that might most be feared for that reason are among the higher class of magazines, and those which from the point 14011-186
of view of their moral standard we would never think of objecting to; and that magazines that are really salacious in character and that we would like to exclude from Canada are not to be feared from that standpoint at all?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I appreciate the attitude
of my hon. friend. Would he call the Saturday Evening Post the better class of United States magazines? I believe my hon. friend is speaking of the Geographic or Harper's or the Century. All these papers sell at a price of twenty-five or fifty cents a copy and a duty of ten cents a pound would not mean anything to them at all. The publisher could absorb the duty, or if he did not, the Canadian purchaser would not object to paying it. We want those high class magazines in this country. I do not believe they are as dangerous as the [Saturday Evening Post, for instance, which is the most dangerous from the standpoint of penetration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
From the standpoint of
morals?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, from the standpoint
of making our young people believe that the United States is the place to live in. This is true not only of the stories but of a number of articles that appear in this magazine. Then there are the Cosmopolitan, True Stories- three hundred Of them, all telling the same story: "Come over to the land of the free, the land of promise."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon.
member mind going a little further and specifying some of the publications which he would characterize as belonging to the class of villainous literature?

friend a long list of them if I had time, but for the moment I will mention Snappy Stories.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I was thinking of
others. One that goes into many homes is the Ladies Home Journal, which I presume is one of the outstanding United States publications. Does the hon. member regard that as undesirable, or not?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not at all undesirable from the moral standpoint.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member, I take it, objects to certain American magazines on two grounds, first, for moral reasons, and secondly because they purvey American sentiment. Would he exclude papers of the type to which I refer?



The Budget-Mr. Hocken

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not arguing for the
exclusion of anything that is not obscene and immoral. I would admit the Ladies Home Journal, which is an excellent publication; but I do say that it ought to pay a tax. But one of the arguments against the Ladies Homo Journal is that, to a larger extent even than the Saturday Evening Post, it is an advertising medium, and as such affects our business relations. I do not think that it is pernicious on the ground of denationalizing our Canadian sentiment. If it does this it is only to a very small degree. I repeat, I believe the Ladies Home Journal to be an admirable publication.	But why should we not have a
Canadian woman's home journal? As a matter of fact we have one published in Toronto by the Consolidated Press, and if that paper were not obliged to compete with the Ladies Home Journal it would do twice the business; it would be twice its present size and its advertisers would derive twice the benefit they now get from it.

speechtext:

gentleman, as a publisher, give us an idea of what it would cost to produce in Canada a paper of the style of the Ladies Home Journal?

It could be nothing but a rough guess, But I should say that to produce
100,000	copies it would cost probably $50,000 or $60,000, and you could not raise the price of advertising in Canada to enable you to secure that revenue. The manufacturers in Canada could not afford to pay the advertising rates that would make the publication of such a magazine feasible, whereas in the case of the Saturday Evening Post the advertisers pay as high as $7,000 and $8,000 a page. Why, it was computed that in one issue of that journal a short time ago there was over $1,000,000 worth of advertising. It was a little larger in volume than the magazine I have here, and the rates were so enormous that in that one issue the advertising amounted to the total I have mentioned.

speechtext:
In that case a
magazine of that kind, if produced in this country under present conditions, would have to be sold at thirty or forty cents per copy.
