speechtext:
One more question and I am through. Do I understand the hon.

member to advocate putting on such a tax as would raise the price of a publication of that description to thirty, forty or fifty cents?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend will see in Hansard, what I have advocated is that section 169 of the tariff be enforced, and that we be given 25 per cent protection. However, if my hon. friends opposite are not willing to concede 25 per cent, then 5 p.m. they might give us 15 per cent or 10 per cent. At any rate, let them give us something, so long as they acknowledge and adopt the principle of protecting the Canadian publisher, not only for his own sake but-because this goes much further than the welfare of the individual-for the good of Canada as a whole. Those men who have money invested in Canadian magazines can withdraw it and go into something else, as in fact they have done. They do not suffer materially; they may lose some money, but they can go into something else. But it is the great masses of the people that suffer, and that is my principal objection.
I have a wThole mass of material disclosing the views of Canadian newspapers, and while I will not read very extensively from it, there are two or three things which I think should certainly be put on Hansard. For instance, I take the following from the Vancouver Morning Star:
The Morning Star in a recent cartoon, pointed out how the very children of Canada are being led away across the border, in their mind at least, by a new Pied Piper in the guise of the cheap American magazine. The menace of this seduction to national distinction, national aspiration, national pride, and even national independence is serious. The mentality and morale of impressionable young Canadians, which should be kept clean and apart to their own land, is being merged in the reeking gas cloud of the lower Americanism. Crime featuring and salacious magazines from across the line are flooding every Canadian news-stand and book shop so that one is hard put to it in the pile of them to pick out a single copy of a Canadian, or even of a British magazine. Something should be done and done quickly to dam this trash which is flowing over the border; demoralizing trash which is deplored by the best type of Americans as well as by Canadians.
I went into a news-stand in Toronto on one occasion and asked for a copy of MacLean's magazine, and although the storekeeper had not a single copy in his place he had, stretched across a large frame on one side of the store, about 100 American magazines. He had not a single Canadian magazine on sale, because he could make more profit out of his salacious literature.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where was that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In my own city, but I presume the same is true everywhere. I have

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
figures here showing that some 2,000 copies of one magazine alone are sold in Ottawa. The newspaper goes on:
When Canadian politicians adopt the new national policy of preventing the export of raw materials to American manufacturers in order to make them make them in Canada then Canada will have, among other things, the best and cheapest paper in the world, because she has the best and cheapest supply of wood pulp.
The article is a column long but I will not read further from it. Let me now quote a few words from Saturday Night:
The Canadian field for Canadian periodicals and in a measure Canadian newspapers is being lost. That is to say our periodical press is being strangled to death by United States competition. There are printed today in Canada a far less number of publications than was the case when our population was half of what it now is, and those that are left are struggling for an existence for the most part. . .
Slowly but surely Canadian publications are being crowded to the wall, and each day the position becomes worse. United States periodicals are practically given away to the readers in Canada, the national advertisers, with headquarters in the United States, footing the bills. Presumably they get their money back by the sale of American goods to Canadians.
A certain United States weekly publication now making a drive tor more circulation in this country is selling for $2 per annum, of which amount $1.80 goes to the canvasser. The white paper in this journal could not be bought in the open market for less than ten cents per copy-
Whether they are referring to the Saturday Evening Post or not, the fact is that there is ten cents worth of paper in this issue I have here.
-to say nothing of the many dollars expended in one way and another before the finished product reaches the reader. And our postmen are becoming round shouldered carrying them around.
What are we going to do about it? Why, nothing of course.
It really looks as if the editor of Saturday Night were in the confidence of the government. They are not going to do anything about it.
It would be a burning shame to place, for instance, a tax on the advertising in United States periodicals coming into Canada.
i think the editor is ironical, Mr. Speaker.
Of course, it would save many millions of dollars now expended for goods, mainly luxuries, made in the United States, and it would add millions of dollars annually to our wage bills, because we could then employ our own people in place of driving them away. Somebody might even have to start a new ink company, or a new type foundry, or a new paper mill or two. And lastly, but not least, we might teach our people to be steadfast Canadians in place of secessionists.
In a generation simon pure Canadian publications, with very few exceptions, will be scarce as the dodo. They simply cannot survive under such conditions.
But I want to give another quotation. This is from the Globe, that old Liberal journal which is eighty years old and still going strong. It says:

Sooner or later the Canadian government will be obliged <to take cognizance of the vast circulation of United States publications dn this country. They are strangling the publishing industry here, depriving Canadian workers of millions of dollars' worth of employment; they are "Americanizing" Canada by means of the reading material offered; they must have a very grave effect on Canadian industry in general, owing to the tremendous amount of advertising of United States products carried in their columns.
The Orillia Packet says:
By all means let us have a duty on the American publications that are flooding Canada, to the extent of more than a million copies a week. It is one new tax to which no objection can be taken.
The Kitchener Record, with which my hon friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) i3 more or less closely connected, says:
Acting upon the contention that the Canadian publishing trade is suffering from outside competition, the-delegation suggests the imposing of a tariff of 10 cents a pound on all periodicals and week-end magazines entering Canada. It is estimated that the consequent revenue would be approximately $5,000,000.
Now, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance ought to listen to that. Does he want $5,000,000 extra revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly; and I must get
$5,000,000 additional revenue if I am to meet the demands of the city of Toronto for new federal buildings.

Well, the city of Toronto, through its representative, is giving my hon. friend the means of getting the money, and having done that I think there should be no objection to his spending it in that city.
Does my hon. friend know how many tons of Canadian newsprint are used by the American papers that come into Canada?

I am dealing with periodicals and magazines which do not use newsprint. But, Sir, $5,000,000 is a lot of money and we ought to have it.
Now, I am taking up more time than 1 expected to-
Go on.
Does my hon. friend notice that the number was considerably less after the budget was brought down?
What was the date?
I cannot give the exact date at the moment. It was late in the month.
My recollection is that it was during the month of April.
Yes.
These figures are for the month of March.
I was referring to the last week.
The last figure of 452 was only for part of the week ending March 29.
The good news of the budget had gone before.
How did it get out?
A lot of our people had gone also.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Don't wory; they are coming back.
You cannot find them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are
showing up everywhere.

Here is something, Mr. Speaker, that the publishers of Canada have reason to feel aggrieved about. I have a statement signed by the secretary of the Magazine Publishers that it was known in the United States two weeks before the budget was brought down that there was to be no change in the tariff so far as American magazines were concerned. Yet in Canada the men interested in this particular industry could not get a word of information. The publishers' organization in the United States printed a bulletin weeks before this tariff was brought down in which they said they had it on reliable authority that no tax of the kind was going to be imposed. There is the printed document.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me-has he read in the Financial Post of last week the compliments paid to the officials of the Finance and other departments of government because there was absolutely no leak, no person knew what was in the budget until it was brought down?

I can only conclude, Mr. Speaker, that the American publishers have a special aptitude at mind reading, for they issued a bulletin in which they indicated something which absolutely turned out to be correct.
Now, Sir, the moral effect of this flood of magazines is something which we ought to take cognizance of. In this connection let me quote from a letter which appeared recently in the Montreal Gazette, signed by "A Catholic Reader". He says:
It is a pleasure to turn to the fine, public-spirited letter of a Montreal physician, Dr. Korenberg. As a medical man, he states:	"Nothing can so easily and
surely demoralize our children (and grown-ups) as constant reading of scandalous and filthy literature. Constant reading of such journals by our young generation, and by our older generation as well, will tend definitely to mould their character, their opdnions and their outlook on life in a very undesirable (to put it mildly) cast."
Now, what have the Americans to say of their own magazines that are flooding this country? This is written by Frank R. Kent, the Washington correspondent of the Baltimore Sun, and it appeared in The Independent, a journal published in Boston:
"And not only have we produced a great smut crop of a coarseness peculiarly our own," he says, "but the more obscene of the French papers have now been translated into English and appear on the news stands along with the originals. When you stop to analyse, scrutinize, and cheek up, there is here presented more reason for apprehension as to the future than any other single symptom in America to-day.
"The place to fully appreciate its proportions-"
And this applies to Canada quite as much as to the United States.
"-is in the smaller cities and towns, with populations ranging from 20.000 up to 100,000-towns, for instance, like Fairmont, West Virginia-"
Or we might say Hamilton, Ontario:
-where one news dealer sells 2,200 copies of every issue of a single monthly, exclusively devoted to stories of sex experiences and the nude in art; or like Steubenville, Ohio, where out of 110 periodicals on sale in a single store, 60 were either out and out a prurient type or bordered on the libidinous line.
"It is not the cheap and sexually suggestive fiction magazines, although these are many and rotten, that constitute the real shock troops of these paper battalions of literary indecency so much as the smaller and more compact non-fiction affairs frankly and exclusively given over to obscenities. Some of these are published in Chicago, some in Philadelphia, but most of them in Newark, New Jersey, and are issued by the same individuals under different corporate names. They mainly contain a rehash of the dirty stories and jokes told in the smoking rooms of puQlman cars or hotel lobbies.
"If you want to know whether these things are widely read, all you have to do is check up with any intelligent news dealer dn any city, big or little, in any part of the country. The candid ones will not hestitate to tell you, not only that the demand for this sexual literature is enormous, but that there is no such thing as oversatisfying it. Those who buy

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
one of these periodicals will buy every similar one on sight. The more you feed it, .tihe keener it gets. That is why there is a constantly increasing number of these things. As fast as one lewd venture is launched and successfully established, a little twin brother, under a different name and in a dress of a different colour, is sent out and is equally successful with the same clientele."
That is the kind of stuff a large part of which is coming into Canada free, because of the conflict in the items in the customs tariff, and that is the kind of stuff that our young people should be protected from. If it is not the duty of the government to protect the people of this country from that kind of thing, I would ask the members of the administration, who else will do it? How is it to be done? To my mind, it is one of the most important duties the government has to perform.
I go this far, Mr. Speaker. If there is one thing under modern conditions that a nation should endeavour to do, it is to establish and develop a periodical press. I base my argument, Sir, upon this fact, that to a very large extent the periodical press has taken the place of books. A very much larger and increasing proportion of our people all over the country are reading magazines and periodicals of various kinds. The amount of book reading is less in proportion to-day than it ever was, and it is due to the periodical press taking the place of books to a very large extent. It is possible for a periodical press to develop national sentiment in a way that no other form of publication can do. It goes out weekly or monthly, it contains articles building up the national sentiment, strengthening the national spirit, and it goes to the people who read it this week, and next week, and the next week, all through the year. Like drops of water constantly falling upon a stone, it makes an indelible impression. The young mind filled with national sentiment built up by the reading of a Canadian periodical press would remain forever Canadian, but if, instead of being cultivated by a Canadian press, the young mind is cultivated by an American press, it acquires American ideas instead of Canadian ideas. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that the young people of Canada to-day know more about President Coolidge than they do about the right hon. leader of this government. The name of Mackenzie King is not in literature that is read in Canada as much as the name of President Coolidge.
Not in Ontario?

Not in any part of the
country. Besides, Mr. Speaker, this is not a joking matter, as I see it. I may be all astray in my opinion, but to my mind this is
one of the most serious questions that a government can take up. If we are not to protect the young people from obscenity, which is our duty; if we are not to make law3 that will develop and strengthen national sentiment, how can we expect that Canada will remain Canada? If we want to protect our people and provide against a secessionist sentiment, we must get our young people to learn what Canada means to them, what we have in Canada, and why Canada should be built up. Teach them that Canada is as good a country to live in as there is in the world, if not better. But we are not teaching them that, and we are allowing our neighbours to the south to teach them something entirely different.
I say, Sir, that the periodical press occupies a position in the world to-day that it never did before, and Canada has no periodical press. Canada ought to have one, and Canada can only get one if there is a certain degree of encouragement given in restricting the flood from a neighbouring and a foreign nation, and then providing, so far as can reasonably be provided, for a flood of Canadian periodicals.

May I ask a question? The hon. gentleman has been very fair to us so far, and I hope he will extend this courtesy to me. A moment ago I asked a question with respect to stories appearing in Hearst publications being reprinted in MacLean's Magazine. The hon. member replied that MacLean's reprinted only stories by Canadian authors. The hon. member was w'rong. I have in my hand MacLean's Magazine of the issue of March 15, in which there appears a story entitled "Here Comes the Bride," by Fanny Hurst, a story of the Bowery, the East side of New York City, reprinted from the Cosmopolitan.
I am not acquainted with the lady. I do not know whether she is a Canadian or not.
I am informed that she is a United States Jewess.

If it is a particularly fine
article and it does not affect our national spirit I do not see why MacLean's should not publish it. But Mr. MacLean's idea, as expressed to me personally, is to develop and encourage Canadian writers. By reason of the Copyright Act you can get the works of Canadian waiters, and so far as possible, he gets Canadian writers in his paper in every case rather than American writers. He is a strong Canadian, a strong imperialist, and he as much as any man in this country is trying to stem the tide of this avalanche of American publications.

I want to point this out to the House: We are a young country, we are yet in the formative stage. Our future depends upon the present and the rising generation, more so perhaps than is the case in most other countries. That makes it increasingly important for us to see that the present and the rising generation are not denationalized in sentiment, but that on the contrary they should have their Canadian spirit and Canadian sentiment highly developed. So that we are perhaps in a different position from any other country in the world in that respect. We are to-day laying the foundations, and they must be laid in the minds and in the hearts and in the intellects of the people; that is the only foundation for a nation. I venture to say, Sir, that the province of Quebec is the only province in the confederation that can be said to-day to have its ideals fixed, and that is due to the fact that it has been made impervious to American influences. Premier Taschereau told us a short time ago that the attitude of the people of Quebec to day was the same as it was three hundred years ago. That makes them impervious to this Americanizing. Then again, all these magazines are printed in English, which is not read fluently by a great many people of the province of Quebec. Therefore these American magazines cannot permeate that province in the way in which they can all the rest of the provinces. But every other province in confederation is in a state of flux so far as its national sentiment is concerned. That sentiment is not fixed, and it is being fed by the *most pernicious anti-Canadian literature that is printed anywhere in the world. We are rapidly imbibing American ideals, and that must inevitably weaken and ultimately destroy that definite Canadian sentiment which it is *our duty to strengthen. If Canada is not to 'be absorbed by the republic our government must take measures to protect our people from this infiltration of Americanism.
We all deplore the exodus of our young people across the border; it is an economic loss that no country can stand for any length of time. The first members of a family who cross the line act as a sort of magnet to all the other members of the family, drawing them at one time or another to the substantially better conditions that are said to prevail in the United States. In my opinion the flood of American periodicals that enter Canada is doing nothing more or nothing less than rob this Dominion of its native-born citizens who have free and unlimited entry to the republic. All they have to do is to get a certificate of birth, and over they go without 
any further question. We are being left with a population born elsewhere than in Canada, much of it very desirable, some of it not quite so desirable. In any event a Canadian-born citizen has greater potential value to this country than a man from any other part of the world. If there is any of the population we should endeavour to preserve, it is the native-born Canadian, and we are not doing that.	.
I am not arguing that our relations with tin United States should be any other than inti mate and friendly. We have lived beside then for over one hundred years without any dispute that could not be settled by arbitration Our social, our business, our fraternal relations with the United States are about as intimate in the case of some provinces and states as are the relations between the different provinces of Canada. I have no objection to that; I wish to encourage it. I happen to belong to two or three international organizations myself. But it is one thing to maintain friendly and intimate relations of that character, and it is something entirely different to allow our young people to be tempted or to be influenced in such a manner that they come to think more highly of the United States than of their own country. Unless we are willing to watch our country drift into annexation with the United States we must do something to strengthen a national Canadian sentiment, and as I have argued before, nothing will be so effective in enabling us to do that as a strong Canadian periodical press that . will emphasize the advantages of our own country and make 'Canadians proud of their native land. We should, as far as possible, guard against the cultural as well as the economic penetration of this country by the United States.
To those who favour our absorption by the republic to the south my argument will have no weight; but with all who desire that Canada should remain a member of the British commonwealth this must be a question of the first importance. I present it to the House not for the first time or for the second time. I urge the government once again to sit down quietly and consider solemnly the ramifications, the evil results that are following and will increasingly follow the continued free entry of American magazines into this country.
I realize the differences we have in Canada, yet I believe we have an opportunity to build up one of the greatest countries in the world. We have the soil, we have the resources of all kinds, and we have a climate that ought to make men just a little better than they are in

any other part of the world. But we can only succeed if we make Canadians proud of their country-so proud of it, in fact, that they will be willing to make some little sacrifice to live in this Dominion. Unless we can do that the great republic to the south, with its 110,000,000 of people, with its better financial opportunities awaiting all the time, will attract the very cream of our population. Mr. Speaker, the remarks that I wish to address to the House on this occasion will be directed not so much towards the budget itself as towards certain criticisms that have been made of it, and trade conditions in general in Canada. It is not my purpose so much to build up a constructive argument as to endeavour to show up some of the fallacious arguments that have been used. If we can do that I think perhaps we shall have laid in some measure the foundations for a better understanding of the situation that confronts us.
I might make a few remarks, however, upon the budget itself. I shall not refer at all to the general financial situation; but speaking of the matter of trade conditions in Canada it has been pointed out, and very properly so, that the satisfactory conditions that prevail in this country are dependent in large measure upon the splendid harvests that have been reaped by the farmers in all parts of the land. It is only natural of course that the government should be pleased that the two conditions should have coincided-that is, the continuance of the government in office and the splendid harvest that has been reaped. It is only natural that hon. members on the government side should refer to that fact with pride and take some satisfaction out of it. On the other hand it is only natural that their opponents should belittle as much as possible the activities of the government and give all the credit to Providence. Now, we in the west who have received these large crops recognize that Providence has blessed us wonderfully during the past two years. We also recognize that the large exports of wheat that are going forth from this land have been brought about by the co-operation of Providence with the hard-working diligent farmers of the Canadian west.
I should like to call attention again to some very wise remarks that were made by the
hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) in which he showed the position which the Canadian west is occupying now in the economic life of the Dominion. Perhaps this was never more strongly stated than in an address that was given by Sir Henry Thornton, president of the Canadian National Railways, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of Saturday, January 9, 1926. This address was delivered in November last, and I wish to refer to only two or three sentences. He points out in the course of this address that during the early part of last year the Canadian National Railways did not show a very strong position as regards the business done, but that towards the middle of the year conditions began to improve. He then goes on to say:
About the middle of July, however, a definite firm undertone in Canadian business began to manifest itself, so that the decrease in gross earnings has now been wiped out and an increase in gross of approximately $7,000,000 will be shown at the end of the year.
At the beginning of July it was perfectly manifest there was going to be a magnificent harvest in the west, and naturally that made itself evident in the immediate increase of the business of the country. Again he says:
The crop conditions for the year undoubtedly helped the position, but a large measure of success is due to the healthy growth of business in general in all parts of the Dominion. Because of the important part played by 'the crops in Canada's general business conditions it seems inadvisable to go beyond the first six months of next year in venturing any predictions. Given an average crop, however, I believe that the sound undertone which has made itself felt in Canadian business during the latter half of 1925 will continue to increase in strength during the first half of 1926.
Perhaps it might not be amiss for the government and all of us to take the warning given by Sir Henry Thornton when he said that it might not be wise, in the matter of predictions, to go beyond the first six months of the year-another recognition of the fact that the prosperity of Canada is very closely bound up, indeed absolutely dependent upon, the prosperity of the farm.
It is a matter of pride on the part of all Canadians that our National railway has reached the status that it has now attained. For my part-and I think I speak for those, in the main, who sit in this comer of the House-we never criticized the action of the government of the day in taking over the railway lines and beginning the amalgamation of them into a united whole. We recognized that it was a matter of necessity that such a step should be taken, and for my part I am inclined to give credit to those who controlled the government of the day. But when these lines were taken over they were
The Budget-Mr. Brown

not in a position to compete effectively with the Canadian Pacific railway, and while hon. members claim that credit should be given to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) for having brought about the amalgamation, we should also remember that he has taken the position that we should not spend one dollar more in the way of equipment. I think he has used expressions of that kind on different occasions. We in this House have voted large sums of money during the past few years for the equipment of the National lines, and that equipment is now such that the railway will become a very effective competitor with the Canadian Pacific. For the next few years I do not think it should be necessary to spend any very considerable amount in equipment in order to make it possible for the Canadian National to compete with the other road.
I had intended to speak at some length on the question of the income tax, but the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) expressed pretty nearly my sentiments in regard to that matter. It is seemingly a popular move that the income tax should be reduced. I note with approval, however, that the government has acted in certain respects as some of us have argued during the past few years. I notice with particular pleasure the provision in regard to the tax upon dividends. We have been arguing that distinction should be made between revenue derived from investment and revenue derived from salaries or from business. For my part I cannot agree with the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion); I cannot work up a great deal of sympathy for that hypothetical widow who has to pay an increased tax on an income of $5,000 Which she receives from dividends. There are a great many widows in the country for whom I have a great deal more sympathy than the widow who receives an income of $5,000 from her husband's estate.
I would like to commend the government for taking a step in the direction of another principle we advocated, namely, that for the purposes of taxation the income of the husband and wife should be considered a joint income. They have not perhaps gone as far in that respect as some of us have advocated, but a step has been made in that direction and I think the policy is eminently sound.
It is quite obvious that different views are held by hon. members in this House in regard to these matters. One feature of the income tax as set forth in the proposed change was condemned by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie), and that is the feature that made the strongest appeal to me as praiseworthy. The hon. 
member criticized the proposal that carrying charges on unproductive property should no longer be exempt. I commend that change most heartily. I do not see why a man speculating in land, for instance, or having any other unproductive property, should be allowed to deduct the carrying charges when he makes his claim for exemption.
The postal reductions have been received generally with a measure of favour, and perhaps the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) expressed what was a very common attitude toward the postal service when he said it was one that should be rendered to the people at cost, and that the government should not make any excessive profit out of it. I know that that position is very generally taken by people, and I am not going to combat it; but I would like to present another point of view to which we might give some consideration. It should be remembered that the government is rendering many services to the country at less than cost. It might very well be argued, if that is the case that some of these services which show a small profit might be continued in order that other unproductive services might be continued-provided always of course that these services should not be in any degree burdensome on the-country. That, to my mind, is a point of view that might very well be considered..

"I do not speak the language of resentment or of bitterness. I speak only the language of truth when I say that never in the history of elections in this Dominion has a great party stooped to methods at once so dishonest and so dangerous as did the Liberal party in the late campaign in the province of Quebec/' declared the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, Conservative leader, speaking at a banquet given here to-night by the Wentworth Conservative Association in honour of

Gordon C. Wilson, member-elect for Wentworth. "While the Prime Minister," said Mr. Meighen "was talking unity in English-speaking Canada, and was presenting himself as its only true guardian and apostle his lieutenants were adopting every means known to the platform speaker or the pamphleteer to stir up all the old war animosities and to conjure new fears and new hostilities in the minds of the good people of Quebec."
In reply to this statement may I read part of an article headed "The Conservative Party" published in September, 1924, before this famous Hamilton speech?
Is the protectionist party poorly led? The late election (St. Antoine) seems to supply an affirmative
answer	A gathering of Conservatives weddeu
to protection from which men of note like Mr. Sauve and his eminent colleague, Mr. Patenaude-

Leadership is not all, but it is much, as the radiant eras of Macdonald and Laurier attest. Few possess the personal magnetism which compels confidence and loyalty, and the golden tongue of oratory, and we cannot hope to soon look upon the like of these men again.
A convention of delegates drawn from all parties of Canada should be summoned in order that a declaration of principles be drawn up. a spirit of cooperation and confidence cultivated, local leaders consulted, and free expression given to party preference on the subject of leadership. I would like my hon. friends opposite to note those words-
-and not by selection by representative delegates, and it may well be worth while trying the latter method. That is not taken from Le Soleil or Le Canada, but from the Montreal Gazette, whose chief editor at that time was the present member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) in this House, a firm supporter of the right hon. leader of the opposition.

If the hon. gentleman will allow me, the hon. member for Mount Royal is no longer the editor of the Gazette.
He was editor when this article was written on September 9, 1924.
One of the editors.

The article reads:
The Conservative party, under its present leaders, is beaten now, before the next general elections start.
This was published, not in Le Soleil or Le Canada, but in the Quebec Chronicle, a Tory paper, of September 30, 1924.
I have another quotation from a letter to the Montreal Gazette, dated December 10, 1924, also before the famous Hamilton speech. I will read only the most interesting part of the letter, which I am sure several hon. members have already read. It is also entitled "The Conservative Party," but it is not written by a Liberal:
His defects (Mr. Meighen's) seem to lie in his apparent indifference to changes of public opinion, his dislike of new ideas, his reluctance to analyze current economic problems to which he is not accustomed and which tend to disturb the fixity of his own preconceived opinions, and his seeming lack of discernment and tact in dealing with his fellowmen.
Another apparent defect in Mr. Meighen's leadership is his overweening desire to preserve a semblance of personal consistency in his political opinions. The electors are only slightly interested in the aberrant mental growth of any individual, whether he be leader of the government or of the opposition.
Yet when Mr. Meighen comes to Quebec, his addresses seem to sound a note of challenge to each of his hearers to find any flaw or fault in the conduct, during the war, of the administration of which he was a member; and he thus provokes a division and vote upon issues which had best be deemed dead and buried and upon which he can never hope to procure in this province a popular verdict favourable to himself and to his colleagues of the old regime.
The Conservative electors of this province frequently express regret that the Conservative leader seems to regard the consistency of his own personal history as of so much more vital importance than the future progress and prosperity of the country, that, instead of utilizing existing conditions as a means of restoring the Conservative party to place and power, he ignores the problems of the present and creates widespread distrust by diverting public attention to the dead issue* of the past in respect to which he may never expect the approval of a large majority of the Quebec con-, stituencies.
As I said, this was published in the Montreal Gazette of December 10, 1924, and after having read that I am sure the right hon. leader of the opposition must have said to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, "Tu quoque, Brute."
The other day my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) quoted a letter from a gentleman of the province of Quebec about home-made carpets. I asked him if the letter came from Mr. Patenaude, and he said:
No, but I do say this, that a lot better things come from Mr. Patenaude than from my hon. friend, judging by some of the speeches he has delivered in this House.
Well, I may be able to please my hon. friend from Fort William this time by quoting

and allowing him to read in Hansard tomorrow morning, as he is not in his seat at the moment, a false argument made by Mr. Patenaude himself in his maiden speech at St. Laurent last fall, on the 19th of September. In that speech, which has been reported by all the papers, Mr. Patenaude stated two things which are contradictory, and which show his insincerity. First he said:
I do not intend to create a third party.
Next he said:
I am free of Mr. King aa well as of Mr. Meighen.
Now these two things are contradictory. If he was not going to create a third party, iiow could he be independent of Mr. Meighen and Mr. King? That is very hard to understand. May I quote to the House what took place at a joint meeting held during the last election?
A man in the audience asked:
If it is true that you are free of Mr. Meighen as well as of Mr. King, on which side, you Patenaude candidates, will you sit in the House?
We will stand up.
Anybody familiar with the rules of the House knows that no hon. member can stand in the House while another member has the floor. But so few Patenaude candidates were elected that this statement is not of any consequence. A man in the audience said:
"You say you will stand up if you are elected. That is too tiresome. To give you a change to rest we will force you to stay home."
Now, Sir, what was the real purpose of Mr. Patenaude in running as Liberal Conservative leader in the province of Quebec? Was he influenced by motives of patriotism? Did he act as the result of money considerations? No, I think it was capitalism that pushed him into the fight. The matter is very well explained in an article in the Montreal Gazette, and it seems that I am destined to quote mainly from Tory papers to-night. The article in question appeared in the Montreal Gazette of September 22, 1925, and contained the following statement:
Mr. Patenaude has entered the federal field to turn out the King government.
This with respect to a man who is supposed to be independent. The article goes on to say:
He has no praise for its work, no respect for its policy of drift, only contempt for politicians without stable views who count noses before they determine lines of legislation. Mr. Patenaude is not a Janus.
I do not know who wrote that article. I do not know whether it was the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) or somebody

else. Whoever the writer was he made a big mistake because if Mr. Patenaude was not a Janus he did not always tell the truth. I continue quoting:
He has not two faces looking in opposite directions, but is a man of fixed convictions and firm resolution, fit to be trusted. His platform is made of Conservative planks. While steadfast in support of the constitution and of the rights of Quebec, in the broad spirit as well as the narrow letter o<f that charter, he believes, as he well may, that a prosperous and contented French-Canadian province contributes enormously to the prosperity and contentment of the whole Dominion, in the general welfare of which he is deeply concerned. His return to a larger arena of political activity-
His return was stopped, by the way. -than he has recently engaged in is one of the most hopeful signs of the day, hopeful for the success of Conservative principles, hopeful for new policies in government, hopeful for the hush of provincial strife and the burying of issues long dead. It is the present and the future that concern Canadians. They are in a rut. The country drifts without strong leadership and sage counsel, such as men of the type of Mr. Patenaude can supply. Behind him, we bedieve, will rally men of good purpose and strong patriotism, men who are convinced that conditions cald for change of government. To all these the new provincial leader appeals for support, and that appeal, we are confident, will not be made in vain.
It has been made in vain. How did Mr. Patenaude's friends try to turn out the King government? The story is very interesting. I will read another quotation from the same Tory paper, and the gentleman speaking is not a Liberal but a die-hard Tory, Dr. Thibau-deau, of Two Mountains. His speech was made at a convention to choose a Conservative candidate, and Dr. Thibaudeau, who as I have said is a genuine Tory, expressed himself as follows:
Dr. Thibaudeau said his impression was that Mr. Fauteux, who was too good a man to risk a seat, would have a better chance elsewhere.
He was a bad prophet, that fellow. The report goes on to say:
A hint was then dropped by the speaker about the unpopularity of Hon. Mr. Meighen, for which reason he would support Mr. Frlion, who, being a new man had had no relation with the federal leader of the party.
Mr. Filion is Mr. Patenaude's legal partner, that is the reason why he is such a good man, according to Mr. Thibaudeau. The report goes on to say:
The convention should therefore consider the letter before them as final as regards the decision therein. He supposed, he said, that Hon. Mr. Fauteux had realized the unpopularity of Mr. Meighen would reflect on him in such a way as that it would be impossible to overcome in the country that obstacle to his election.
That- speech was made at the Conservative convention at St. Eustache, and is reported

An old Conservative member from Ontario, very well known for his military and financial activities, was lunching last week with a Montreal friend.
"Colonel, are you interested in the elections? You are a die-hard Conservative."
"Yes, a Conservative, as there are very few now in politics."
"But they say that Mr. Meighen's party is very strong in Ontario."
"Not amongst the out-and-out Conservatives. He is not considered as a Conservative and he ihas none of the characteristics of the true Conservative. He is not safe. He falls into state socialism and seems to be a visionnaire. May I tell you a thing that will perha-ps surprise you; I, an old member, a veteran of politics, who hears the bugle call like an old war
horse, in election time, I go	hunting. And
several friends of mine will do the same. We wish that Mr. Meighen is beaten in his own constituency, sa that we might get rid of him once for all.
These sentiments were uttered by a gentleman clearly indicated as an old Tory member of the province of Ontario. This gentleman's name is not given in the paper but it has never been denied.
He would be a great friend of the leader of the opposition.

Well, I do not know
whether he ever made a horse trade, or whether he ever indulged in horse racing, but what he said is horse sense. Conservatives came before the country with no broken pledges.
This was before the Hamilton speech. May I now give a quotation from the speech of a prominent Conservative gentleman, Mr. Thomas Louis Bergeron. It is reported in Le Soleil, of September 22, 1925. He said:
As for me in the present election, I support the Liberal candidate Mr. Sylvestre. Since 1917 I have fought with you, Liberals, against the ideas of the Conservative leader. Since 1917, did Mr. Meighen abandon his political ideas? I find the same men with him.
And sometimes when I look round at the House I am surprised to see the same men who were with Sir Robert Borden when he
was in the House. I should like to repeat to my hon. friends the old Greek proverb: "Tell me whom you go with and I will tell you who you are." It is old Greek wisdom. Some time ago there was an interesting editorial in the Toronto Mail and Empire. I went to the library to get it, but I found that the page had been cut out of the file. I was able to find the editorial, however, in a French paper, and I will give an extract from it in English for the benefit of my hon. friends: Referring to the leader of the opposition, this was published in the editorial page of the Toronto Mail and Empire of December 14, 1925, page 28:
He does not presume to tie his party up to a mode of procedure that has his present-day approval.
Some time ago my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) made a short speech of five hours. I asked him when he adjourned the debate on Wednesday afternoon if he would be good enough to read also a part of his Toronto speech. This was a great speech, and I note it was published in ex-tenso in the Montreal Star the same day it was delivered in Toronto; that is good information service. I read from Hansard of February 17, as follows:
Mr. Pouliot: "Would the hon. member be good enough to read also part of his Toronto speech?
Mr. Cahan: As it is now six o'clock, I will reserve that for to-morrow, when I am perfectly willing to read the whole of it if the hon. gentleman will repeat his question.
As I did not repeat the question and he did not read the speech, I will have the pleasure of dealing with it myself. I have here a copy in extenso of the report in the Montreal Star of December 8, 1925.
Do you not think it was a very good speech?
I cannot judge of it, and I must leave it to the House to judge. I am sorry the right hon. leader of the opposition is not here. He is the man who could judge of the appropriateness of the speech.
What is your opinion?
I am sorry that some hon. members speak in a Liberal way and vote in a Conservative way.
When has any issue embodied in the Hamilton speech ever been before this House in a vote?
Louder, please.

The hon. member insinuated with respect to myself that I speak in a Liberal way and vote in a Conservative way.

I ask the hon. member whether that applied to my speech. Was that not a good Conservative speech, and does it not meet with the approval of the Liberals of the province of Quebec also?
I am very sorry that my hon. friend speaks against his leader and votes with him. That is the point. If he spoke in a Liberal way, how is it he never supported the Liberal party in this House?
The government has never introduced a real Liberal measure in this House to be voted upon since I came here.
It is a very funny thing that when my hon. friend goes to Toronto, which is a Tory city, he thinks Liberal, and when he is in Ottawa he thinks Conservative.
When he is in Toronto he speaks good Conservative doctrine and when he is in Ottawa he also speaks good Conservative doctrine, and in the province of Quebec he speaks also in the same way.
I shall be very glad tc read his speech myself.

The right hon. leader of the opposition would be a little surprised at the language used by my hon. friend in Toronto, where he had no reason to meet with any kind of obstruction. On December 8, 1925, a year after the famous letter in the Montreal Gazette which has been quoted, he made that speech. It is directed against the leader of the opposition. It was late in the fall, just before the winter. This seems to be a yearly occurrence. I will read it:
It may be that the personal policy which Mr. Meighen recently announced at Hamilton, and more recently at Bagot, may temporarily turn the tide of local sentiment; but speaking also personally, with a quite intimate knowledge of the views and sentiments which generally prevail in the province of Quebec-
What does my hon. friend know about the sentiments which prevail in Saint Jean de Dieu, Notre-Dame du Lac and Saint Paul de la Croix?
Does the hon. gentleman want a reply to that?
Yes.

I think that generally speaking I know the sentiment of Quebec quite as well a3 my hon. friend. I knew the sentiment of Quebec before he was born. I have lived

there and been in contact with a large part of Quebec as long as he has, and I think the statements I have made with regard to the sentiment of Quebec are amply justified.

I will continue; I am very sorry for the interruption because it breaks the Charm of the quotation:
I do not believe that the Hamilton pronouncement will be regarded, either in Quebec or in the other provinces of Canada, as binding upon the conscience and judgment of the Conservative party as a whole, nor as controlling the discretion of parliament, whenever grave international complications may arise in the future. Nor do I believe that such a pronouncement made by a political leader, however able and esteemed he may be, will serve to remove permanently the estrangement which at present exists between Quebec and the majority of the provinces outside of Quebec.
This is honey or maple syrup in a barrel of vinegar.
Personally, I am confident that a clear understanding could be reached by which these vital interests could be dealt with effectively by the Conservative party of Canada, which has now the largest representation in the House of Commons, but that end and object can only be attained by maintaining unity and solidarity of the Conservatives throughout all Canada-
I do not know whether it i3 by speaking against the right hon. leader of the party that my hon. friend wanted to promote conj fidence amongst the members of the party. The letter continues:
-and, more than that, the unity of the Conservative party in Canada can only be maintained if and so long as the leader or leaders of the Conservative party shall avoid all mere temporary expedients.
The right hon. leader of the opposition must know that this comes from one of his supporters, one of his best friends who always votes for him. I would not dare believe that if it had not come from a Tory. If a Liberal had said that to me, I would have answered: You do not know Mr. Meighen. Mr. Meighen must be better than that. But this comes from one of his closest friends, a man who has voted with him since the beginning of this session, so what can I say. I say: He knows him very well; it must be true. What I would not believe from another fellow, I am bound to believe when it comes from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). He says he knows the people of Quebec very well. He is a psychoanalyst; he has studied psychology and he must know the leader of the opposition very well. When his name is mentioned in the papers, he is called not only by his first name and his family name, but it is always Mr. So-and-So, the eminent Montreal lawyer. I do not think that kind of lawyer defends his leader very much even in Ontario. I do not like to be disagreeable to my hon. friend;

I respect him very much and this is why I am surprised that he has revealed such a secret. This is not what happened to Noah. When Noah was drunk, his sons were told to bring a blanket to cover him, but my hon. friend uncovers his leader. This is perhaps why he has lately defended the sale of liquor. The hon. member continued:
But that end and object can only be attained by maintaining unity and solidarity of the Conservatives throughout all Canada, and, more than that, the unity of the Conservative party in Canada can only be maintained if and so long as the leader or leaders of the Conservative party shall avoid all mere temporary expedients and all off-hand and captious decisions, and shall call to their councils for the due consideration of these questions the representatives of all sections of this wide Dominion.
Is it not great? This is one of the best orations I have ever read in my life.

What objection does the
hon. member have to it?

I have this objection, that I think party supporters must have respect for and show loyalty to their leaders. That is my point. I show loyalty to my leader;
I am ready to defend him because I am proud of him. If my hon. friend is not satisfied with his leader, the only thing for him to do is to vote against him, come over to our side and vote with us.

However much I may differ or may have differed from my right hon. leader, he is so far superior to any leader on the opposite side and his measures are so far superior that an independent man could not but endorse them.
I have only one question to ask of my hon. friend. Were my quotations correct?
I think so, as nearly as I can remember.
That is all I want.

Our party is the Liberal
party and we are very glad to defend our leader the Prime Minister, when he is attacked in such a dirty way as he has been attacked in Quebec by some of the Patenaude speakers. I am glad my hon. friend has brought the question up. I will answer him immediately by quoting an extract from a speech
by Mr. L. J. Gauthier, a former member of this House, and I am sure that this extract from his speech will not meet

En remaniant la raaison de Laurier, en vendant sa bi-bliotheque a l'encan, je dis que M. King a porte une main criminelle sur l'idole de la race. La salle ou le grand homme d'etat travaillait a resoudre les problemes angoissants de l'avenir du pays, M. King l'a transformee en une salle de danse.	*

Ma reponse, la voici. Continuez a salir ma reputation; continuez a salir mes cheveux blancs, je conti-nuerai a combattre pour ce que je crois fit-re les meil-leurs interets de mon pays et personne ne pourra m'empecher de proclamer la verity.
May I translate this:
By making alterations to Laurier house, by selling Laurier's books by auction, I say that Mr. King has put a criminal hand on the idol of the nation. Hear, hear.

Continue to throw dirt on my reputation. . . .
This is the way the old dirty scoundrel was speaking:

This is one of the most infamous and direct lies uttered by a filthy liar who suffers from halitosis of speech. Laurier's books never belonged to the Prime Minister. books; they did not belong to him; he never had them in his possesion, but this is the way that fellow-I do not say that gentleman because he is not a gentleman-spoke in the province of Quebec. Many of the people, believing this, sold their potatoes, with the result that they suffered a great loss, while those who held on to their crop have been rewarded with prices of $2, $2.50 and $3. I see by L'Evenement of March IS that potatoes were selling at that time at $2.65, and-on April 27 the price was $3.65.

To preserve and enlarge the Canadian market for Canadian farm products-this Dominion requires an immediate revision of the Canadian tariff on a definitely and consistently protective basis. That such revision should apply to natural products such as farm products, fish and coaJ with no less thoroughness than to manufactured goods.
If I understand English at all, I gather that the right hon. gentleman considered that it would be a boom to the farmers of Canada to have protection, and high protection. Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw):	You contend that if the
tariff is taken off the prices immediately rise?
Mr. Meighen:	We contend it and we know it,
because we see the facts.

It is not at all surprising that in the province of Quebec the Tory party has no considerable following; the fact is easily explained. When Sir Robert Borden was Prime Minister he made an important statement on April 15, 1915, as will be seen at page 2612 of Hansard of that session. I quote:
And let me say now, for the benefit of parliament, and particularly for the information of persons throughout this country who may be concerned in selling supplies or materials to the government, that if any man in Canada, be he Conservative or Liberal, proposes to commit any fraud or imposition upon the government and people of this country, or to be concerned in any attempt for that purpose, especially in connection with the war vote, he should remember that there are courts of justice in this country, and that the doors of the penitentiary are yawning for every man who commits such an offence.
I am free to refer to this matter, for in my own constituency, although I supported a candidate so long as he acted honourably, the moment he did wrong I denounced him, in spite of the fact that he belonged to the same party as myself. I was not in politics then but when he afterwards opposed my election I beat him by some 3,000 votes. He declared that I was a bad Liberal; but what did he do himself in the last election? Why, he supported the Patenaude Tory candidate.
If there are some very nice fellows on the other side of the House there are others who bear the stigma of graft on their forehead, and during the war, while money was spent legitimately in many ways, there was a great deal that was used for purposes of graft. What was done then was disgraceful and if it were necessary for me to-night to give a catalogue of the scandals that occurred between the years 1911 and 1921 my speech would cover a period of years. It would last at least ten years, for session after session during the Borden-Meighen administration some scandal or other was unearthed. That is why the people have no confidence in the Conservative party. There are nice fellows on that side, I admit; indeed I have personal friends among them. But there are also black sheep in the Conservative family. I do not suppose.

They-

I have before me the last annual report of the Canadian National Railways, and it is so satisfactory that I am not surprised it has been so well received by the country. The board of management state that they do not wish to have any political intereference. They are right, and they are not. As the representatives of the people, it is our duty to ask questions about the Canadian National Railways before we vote money on their behalf. Whether they come before the House to ask for money because the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway was over-valued when that road was taken over as part of the National system is not the question. We should know why we are asked to vote that money, and even if some of the information required by members is of a confidential nature we should have it, at
least in a confidential way. We are in the position towards the Canadian National Railways that a banker is towards his client. He is interested in his client's business, and when that client comes to him for a loan, the banker has a perfect right to say, "Well, Sir, I will grant you the loan provided you furnish me with a satisfactory statement of your business." We are pretty much in the same position towards the National railways: we do not ask for information for our own personal benefit, but for the benefit of our constituents and for the country at large. I wish to give a word of praise to Sir Henry Thornton, who seems to be doing his best to conciliate the different interests in the Canadian National Railways. Under his management I am sure the system will to a great extent be a success.
Now a word with respect to the public service. There are some very capable people in the civil service, some who have grown up in it and are interested in their work, a work that enables them to help along the good government of this country. Such public servants deserve praise. But let me say that every civil servant should be judged according to his personal ability and that no secret society interference or other influence should enter into the consideration of his promotion.
Before closing, Sir, I should 'like to direct the attention of the House to two articles which appeared last November in the Montreal Gazette. One refers to an address delivered by Sir John Aird as retiring president of the Canadian Bankers' Association and is entitled "A Hopeful Outlook." The other article refers to the annual report of the Bank of Montreal for the year ending October 31 last, and is headed "An Encouraging Statement " The first article appeared in the Montreal Gazette of November 16, 1925, the second in the issue of November 27, 1925. We can look not only to the editorial page but to the financial columns of every newspaper, whatever may be its political views, and find ample testimony to the fact that Canada is rapidly improving her position, that the hard days are past, and that she is now entering an era of prosperity under the prime ministership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Mackenzie King.)
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, I said that there are nice people on the other side of the House. I do not say that of them all, but of some, those I know best. That is my sincere opinion. While I do not admit the soundness of their programme, I think we should all unite in promoting measures for the national welfare, and I am sure the country would be all the better for this unity of action.

As a new member of this House, though not by any means the youngest, I have thought it my duty not only to my constituents and myself but also, Sir, to you and the other members of this House to sit back and pay heed to the occasional words of wisdom which might' happen to fall from those better versed in parliamentary procedure and in the public business of the country.
I have been much interested and fully occupied in feeling my way about, in endeavouring perhaps, first of all, to learn the first principles of parliamentary procedure; perhaps next, in paying heed to the way in which those members of the administration who occupy seats in this House have sought, though sought in vain, to justify both their right to administer and their administrative acts, activity or inactivity; and next, in observing the way in which those who have criticized the government and its acts have performed their task. I have willingly sat back to listen to the older and more experienced members of this House and, indeed, to very many new members, and when I have observed the splendid way in which all these hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have acquitted themselves, I have felt

that my silence up to this point has been justified.
My constituents, I may say, do not expect me to take a prominent part in the debates of the House. They are very inexacting in this respect. I believe they will be quite satisfied if I do my share in the work they sent me here to do, namely, to give my support to our right hon. leader-and we do not ask lessons from the opposite side of the House as to our leadership; we are all loyally devoted to our venerated leader-in the splendid effort he and his supporters, and in fact the great bulk of the Canadian people, have made and are making to hurl from power the most incapable government this country has yet seen.
I did not come to this parliament imbued with the idea that all of our statesmen of the past have failed to grasp the essential principles of government, nor with the enthusiasm, often misdirected, of youth. I have attempted to read history and to study mankind, and to learn from these studies those lessons which only such studies can teach. We are heirs of the ages and should, from the wisdom of the ages, have acquired some wisdom ourselves. We should not forget that problems as great as we at present are faced with have presented themselves in all past ages since the beginning of time; and that the condition of things existing at present is the composite result of the best minds of all times. Our present constitution is the composite result of the labours of our forefathers and predecessors, arrived at after full discussion of all the pros and cons, and I am satisfied that the works of our forefathers have resulted in a constitution and a set of laws, perhaps not the best, but good enough until we or our posterity can evolve a better; and that we should go slowly in making changes.
What we have is the result of centuries of careful thought and development, and should command and receive some degree of veneration from the present generation, and changes made either in our system of government or in details should not be made hastily or without the best consideration we can give to them; we should not forget, in our haste for change, the struggles of the past from which our present laws have resulted. In this sense I claim to be a Conservative, and I am proud to admit allegiance to the party which adheres to Conservative principles- never averse to change when it is clearly shown that the change is for the better; but until so shown I prefer to stick to what has come down to us as a result of the experience of the ages.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, it was the tariff that was the one and only issue in the good old riding of Brant. Liberal and Progressive speakers take great delight in accusing us of being in favour of a high tariff. This is a false accusation except in so far as it applies to the tariff on poultry and garden produce. On these I say and believe, with my honoured leader and all his supporters, we should apply the motto: "Brick for brick." As for manufacturing industries, however, our motto is: An adequate tariff to insure that an industry run efficiently and economically, shall be able to operate at a reasonable profit and that the tariff adjustments should be made entirely on this consideration.
Much ado is raised over the so-called "big interests." Do the people ever stop to consider that this term is greatly overworked? Nearly all the industries of any magnitude I know of are joint stock companies whose stocks are listed on the exchanges and whose stocks can be acquired on the open market. Few of the industrial stocks are quoted at over par, and anyone with $100 or so to invest can become part owner. As a matter of fact, it can be said of but few of our big industries that they are either one-man companies or

companies in which the stock is held by a few shareholders. The number of shareholders more frequently runs into the hundreds and the thousands. It is a rare thing for a so-called capitalist to invest all his money in one company. He is much more apt to invest in mortgages, bonds or debentures and be content with a smaller, though safer, rate of interest for his money.
I look upon capital as the greatest of blessings to the workingman. You can only get capital out of the hands of the capitalist by giving him the inducement of a larger probable profit from industrial concerns than from such safe investments as mortgages, bonds and debentures.
An adequate tariff which safeguards the investment of capital placed in the hands of efficient management insures work for the workingman, a market for agricultural products, and an adequate rate to the man or group of men who supply the money without which no industry can exist. Some plan of supervision and audit should be devised ' to see that the tariff protection afforded does not permit undue profits to be made or exploitation of the public. When such appear, the time will come for a reduction in the tariff but while this parliament has the power, it would be very unwise for them to exercise the power to make any alteration in the tariff unless and until some one or more experts fully qualified to make a thorough study of the question should advise that the change is desirable, will benefit the public, and will not do an injustice to those interests which are affected by the change. The word "adequate" is the most appropriate word that can be applied to such a tariff.

will appeal to the large masses of wage earners, to the farming communities and to the industrial people who are prepared to take their fair share of the great responsibilities that rest upon every Canadian. The budget speech was a clear and lucid exposition of the situation as it exists in Canada to-day, and it was a budget that cannot fail to make for greater prestige in the near future for this government.
The bringing down of a budget is always a difficult matter. In a country situated as ours is, with our tremendous area and with our interests varied and conflicting in different sections, the sanest and safest course the government can pursue is to elaborate a policy that will bring the greatest good to the largest number. In order to realize the difficulties which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) had to meet when he brought down this budget we have to turn a retrospective glance to the situation as it existed in Canada in 1921 when this government came into power. In 1921 our national debt was about $2,250,000,000; our National railways were creating an annual deficit of over $85,000,000; the merchant marine was costing Canada $12,000,000; we had a situation that was difficult for men engaged in all activities; agriculture was depressed in the west; there was unemployment all over Canada and instability of trade; our currency was depreciated in the markets of the world, and our situation generally was as bad as it had been at any time since confederation.
This year's budget is what I would term a "prosperity" budget. It is a workingman's budget. To-day the labouring man feels the improvement by the size of his savings bank account, and the farmer realizes that there is a general improvement by the high prices he is getting for his farm products. The manufacturer is also feeling the effects of the policy of this government by the increase in the number of his orders, and there is a feeling of confidence in the future and of stability that this country has not experienced since the period of deflation.

We who live in that section of the country, Mr. Speaker, realize what the future development of the immense mineral deposits we have in that north country means for the rest of Canada. We feel we are not exaggerating when we say that the future of the province of Ontario and of Quebec, notwithstanding their present great industrial development, rests in a very large measure upon the development of the tremendously valuable natural resources we have in that country. It is only within the last decade that real development has taken pla«e. Prom the very first start in Cobalt, the discoveries of valuable minerals have extended both east and west of the original discovery, and today in that great pre-Cambrian shield, which contains practically all the valuable minerals known to science, we have a source of greater wealth than is to be found in any other similar extent of territory known to civilization.
Reference has frequently been made in this debate to the woollen industry, and in every instance the present situation in the woollen industry has been attributed to the tariff. As a matter of fact the depression in the woollen industry has been world-wide. Just a few years ago the American Woollen Company, which has practically a monopoly of the woollen industry in the United States was forced, owing to the fluctuating prices of its raw material and to the general depression of the business, to close down one-half of its plants and to turn out of its factories from 15,000 to 20,000 of its employees. Similar conditions exist in Great Britain, where a general depression has existed in the woollen industry. In Canada the depression was felt much more acutely by those engaged in the manufacture of all-wool cloth. In Canada we have a very large number of small mills, but the modern tendency is towards concentration or mass production. In the manufacture of tweed, owing to the variation of styles and patterns, it was impossible for our small manufacturers in Canada to change their patterns or alter their designs as they could in establishments where there was mass production, or production on a very large scale. But there is another factor which has entered into the situation, and which has not yet been referred to in this debate. It is the discovery of a new textile known as rayon. This is becoming to-day an article of general use and its manufacture is progressing, perhaps, at a faster rate than any other industry at the present moment. In the United States rayon has replaced some forty thousand bales of wool annually, but the industry is, as yet, only in its infancy. Hon. gentlemen will have noticed that in the budget the Minister of Finance announces a drawback on rayon silk, or yarn,

Silk versus Artificial Silk in the United States of America
The inroad which the increasing use of artificial silk is making into other textile fields is a subject which comes up for discussion periodically. A few months ago the suggestion was thrown out that artificial silk had displaced 40,000 bales of wool in the woollen in-
dustry, particularly in hosiery manufacture, while similar statements have on various occasions been made by cotton and real silk interests. It is therefore of interest to see from the survey drawn up by the Silk Association of America that there has been a steady increase in silk imports into the U.S.A. for the last 30 years, and consequently of silk consumption in that country, notwithstanding the advent of artificial silk. In 1925, the year when artificial silk output broke all records in the U.S.A., the aggregate number of bales of real silk imported showed an increase of 26 per cent as compared with 1924. It does not appear from these figures that the growing consumption of artificial silk has had any effect on the demand for real silk.
This accounts in a very large measure for the depression that has existed in the knitting industry in recent months in Canada. We have not had sufficient quantities of artificial silk, which has become an absolute necessity to-day. Artificial silk is accepted now as an absolute substitute for real silk, and its manufacture must become in the course of a few years, as I have already said, one of the basic industries of the world. Now, Canada is particularly interested in this industry as pulpwood is the basis of artificial silk.
I have given these few details because I believe in the future of Canada. I think this country has entered upon an era of prosperity such as it has never known before. I believe that the interests of this country will be very much better served, and that emigration may be lessened, if we look at home for the development which is necessary to keep Canadians in Canada. As we look and see the improvements that are taking place daily, and as we view the prosperity that is in store for U3, let each of us, regardless of political affiliations, do our very best for the future development of our beloved country.
